utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. General Talic, can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you and understand you in a language that I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, assisted again today by Denise Gustin to much surprise has come back from holiday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back, and good afternoon to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, for Mr. Brdjanin, I'm John Ackerman along with Marela Jevtovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Good afternoon to you. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you too. So -- yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Ms. Korner used yesterday P882, and she said that this document was found in the 1st Corps documents. But according to the list that was supplied by the OTP, this is a document that would have been given to the Prosecutor's office in June 2000 and which supposedly came from the Croatian files. This is a document that would have been written by the 13th Partisan Brigade because this is a document which comes from Zagreb. We object to it because we don't know how this document arrived in Zagreb and what was the chain of custody of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's right. I've just checked. I tend to rather assume without checking that all military documents come from the 1st Krajina Corps collection, in the sense of being seized from Banja Luka. It's right. It was taken from the Croatian state archives; the reason being, and Mr. Brown is going to be a witness -- is that when the Croatians retook part of them, they also seized part of the military documents. But Your Honour, we can also hear an explanation about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But Madam Fauveau is absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: While I'm on my feet, can I correct something that I said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In relation -- oh, yes, that's right. The OHR report. I told Your Honours that a request to the office of the high representative for an update on the security areas had only resulted in us being sent the 2000 report again. In fact, I made an error. It was put into my room, and I assumed that's what had been sent. In fact, it was the I think UNHCR report which somebody had merely put into my room but it had nothing to do with it. So I made an error. And we're still chasing up the situation with the office of the high representative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Apropos the information that I have, because I chased the matter up as well -- the information that I have is that you should receive a communication updating the risk assessment for 2002. And it should be in your office - when I say "in your office," the OTP's office - by the end of business today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, well, clearly Your Honours have had a splendid effect on that office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It should. That's what I was promised. Now, that stands to be seen, obviously. I mean, I've had many promises in my life.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I believe -- I understand Mr. Ackerman had something to raise. But purely while we're on administrative matters, I don't know whether Your Honours had a chance to consider the transcript of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. I was going to raise that issue myself after posing a question to Mr. Ackerman and Mr. Zecevic. And my question to you is this: Having gone through the transcript which is a transcript of -- a partial transcript of the tape, and having heard what the witness said yesterday, that the commentator is identifiable even with regard to his name at the end of the video recording, something that we were not in a position to confirm or deny because we haven't seen the video recording, are you in a position to confirm, update, or change the position that you made yesterday about the admissibility of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If it pleases the Court, Your Honours. I have checked the tape yesterday in the evening. There are no acknowledgments on the tape either at the very beginning or at the end of the -- of this particular portion of the tape which our learned colleague intends to use. So there is no way we can identify either the commentator or whoever -- the producer of the program or whomever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you agree that at least since the witness said that at some point in time there is also the picture of this commentator which he could identify to us, and since he also said that at the end he is identified, could we at least show that part, whichever part it is - I wouldn't know - to the witness so that he can confirm this? Would you agree to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. But I watched the tape very closely, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm not in any way contradicting what you're stating.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. I haven't seen the commentator. That is what I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I just want to confront the witness now without telling him --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of course we don't have a problem with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you agree to that, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly. I'm just wondering what Your Honour means. What, the witness should sit in court watching it and identify the man to us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. We will ask him the question again, and perhaps someone would prepare the tape according to what the witness will tell us. For example, because the witness yesterday said very clearly at some point in time towards the end there is the -- this commentator is shown in person and then there is -- there is his name later on. So we will --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can do this. What I would suggest as a simple way of doing it, providing nobody objects, is that when the witness finishes today he can be taken to a room where there is a video and simply asked to watch it and point out where he says that is, rather than us all sitting around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can get an investigator to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you agree with that, Mr. Ackerman and Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it's more fun to confront him with it in court, and that's what Ms. Korner is trying to avoid, of course. But I think it's not there, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It may been time consuming in court. Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it would be time consuming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If no one knows exactly except the witness where the relevant part of the video recording is, it will definitely be time consuming.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We're not objecting to this --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- solution from Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So I leave it in your hands. You will take care of that, Ms. Korner, and then we'll deal with it tomorrow. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I mean the only thing that I -- I don't know. It's quite difficult to gauge how long we'll be on the rest of the documents with him. But it might be that I've reached the point where I want to play the video today. So in any event, in which case he can do it in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I'll start -- I'll start with this point again today. Maybe he can be more categoric today. And if that's the case, we will do what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it defeats the whole purpose of the objection if she's just going to play the tape in court and at the end he can't identify the commentator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course not. That's not what I meant. What I meant was putting questions to the witness which would help us identify the part in the -- if there is a part in the video recording which we could show him direct. If it's at the end, just the end of the video recording. And then he should be in the position to tell us, "This is the person I'm referring to."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it, Your Honours, if you -- if you sustain the objection, that the -- the parts that the commentator says will be removed from the transcript before it becomes an exhibit and the -- those parts will also be extracted from the tape before it becomes an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But as I understand it, from what I could understand yesterday, there are two possible relevant parts which one could use to identify who this commentator is. One is, according to the witness, at the end of the video recording there is a list of those who collaborated in its production. That's how I understood it. I may have misunderstood everything, which would not be the first case. The second part is that he said that somewhere -- and I also understood towards the end -- there is a -- a part in which the commentator himself is shown, and he also described him as a person who has gone bald. And so I would like to know where that part -- if it's somewhere in the middle of the video recording, then yes, we will do it as Ms. Korner suggested. He will see it sometime after the sitting today or during a break, have that slot identified, and then we'll see only that slot here together with the end piece of the recording where the names of the collaborators or -- are. And if he can identify it -- if he can identify the broadcast -- the commentator by just looking at this video recording himself without us having the need to go through all this procedure and then tomorrow or later on today he comes forward and says, "The commentator was Mr. Zecevic's brother," then we can carry on from there and we will hand down the decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we have in fact -- I'm sorry, Mr. Ackerman. We haven't in fact argued it. That was the objection that was raised. Then Mr. Filipovic said that he thought the man was on the tape anyhow. But I would wish to submit, Your Honours, it doesn't make a hate worth's of difference whether or not the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, we'll tell you that in our decision basically.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, but we haven't actually -- Your Honours haven't heard any legal argument on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But basically we will understand immediately, as I'm sure Mr. Ackerman has understood already, because that was made abundantly clear yesterday, that if this commentator's identity is established, then practically 94, 95 per cent of the argument he put forward yesterday falls.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I think the whole argument falls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am saying 94, 95 not to be 100 per cent categoric.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, Your Honour, we'll proceed on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Any -- anything else? Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in preparation for the cross-examination of this witness, I have looked at just very briefly a portion of a book by a gentleman named Safer Halilovic where he talked about the Patriotic League which this witness has testified about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And having discovered that, I'm aware that Mr. Halilovic is a -- an accused in this Tribunal, General Halilovic, and that he has, I understand, given very lengthy statements to the Prosecutor. And judging on the content of his book, I would expect that significant portions of those statements are relevant to issues that are being raised in this case and perhaps exculpatory to the defendants regarding some of the issues in this case, certainly some of the statements in his book are. And I understand that those statements might be quite sensitive in some respects. So what I would request is that you order the Prosecutor to give the statements to Your Honours, have you look at this in camera, and determine whether there are any parts of them that you believe are Rule 68 exculpatory kinds of material that ought to be turned over to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I understand the substance of your argument very well. Where I entertain great doubts is how proper -- fit and proper it is for this Trial Chamber to indicate to the Prosecution what falls under Rule 68 and what doesn't when it is absolutely the responsibility of the Prosecution to decide what falls within their obligation to disclose by way of exculpatory material under that rule. I mean, as what you're saying basically means that if in going through these documents in camera, the three of us in our ignorance fail to notice something which is highly exculpatory or partly exculpatory in regard to your clients, we fail to notice it and we fail to indicate it to the Prosecution, then you have no redress against the Prosecution because the Prosecution would have followed our direction or directive. I think it's -- you've sent a message that you think that in these statements there may be exculpatory material, and then it is the duty of the Prosecution once it has this information to go through that material themselves, make an assessment. If they think that there is material -- THE GUARD: Excuse me, Your Honour. We have an emergency in the building. We are going to take the detainees out. Please stay seated. You'll get more information later. We have an emergency in the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This -- we've had this before, Your Honour. This is a fire -- my feeling is once a year they do this. They have a fire drill and they clear the building regardless of what is happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When I'm saying something so important.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. Your Honour, this is I'm afraid to say this is to bring Your Honours down to a level of an ordinary mortal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. It's -- never for a moment do I think that I belong to the other category.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a horrible feeling this is going to be all of us -- I remember this from last year around this time. It will be all of us out of the building for the rest of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But when -- when there are complaints that we keep witnesses here unduly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That we bring them, and that's costing money. And -- Chuqing was not informed about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, it may be a genuine emergency. But it seems to me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we would hear it. No, I'm not hearing any sirens or alarm bells. Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We've been here before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But I was here in November when they asked me to take part in the drill. And I had an appointment that day. But it was at 2.30. Yes. Because I remembered I had an appointment at 2.30 and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think perhaps Your Honour that Ms. Chuqing is the person to ask. Is this a drill or is it genuine.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I really know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I consider -- I mean, you know, it's all very well. I understand fire regulations. But I hope there will be no complaints.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, of course not. I mean, we will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes. So basically -- okay. I'll just wait. So basically what I think is that this is something that the Prosecution ought to take in hand. And I think our responsibility stops there at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, we are joining along with the -- with the -- with the -- asking for our learned colleague Mr. Ackerman and we believe that it is -- it is for the Prosecutor to give us -- to disclose to us the statements of -- or the relevant part of the statements of Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, can I take this in stages. First of all, sometime ago, considerable time ago, the Defence for General Talic wrote to us in respect of the Halilovic and other cases, asking for exculpatory material that -- with a specific list. And we did a check, and I think we gave them some documents. We have never so far been asked to consider what he said in interview. Now, Your Honour, both Defence counsel have known for some time that Mr. Filipovic was going to be a witness and that the Patriotic League was going to be part of it. So can I say this: It's a little late in the day in one respect because this is going to cause a lot more difficulty than I think Mr. Ackerman or Your Honours may perceive. First, I can of course make inquiries about the content of the interview that was held with other members of the Office of the Prosecutor. However, that's not the end of the matter. That, of course, is a confidential matter to that case. And those who represent Mr. Halilovic may have an interest as to whether or not there should be disclosure beyond that. And so therefore we will have to contact, because the contents of that interview of course are confidential. It's not the same as documents which are being disclosed. Now, I don't know -- I know that one of the counsel involved in the case was here today, and it may be because of that, that Mr. Ackerman is raising it. But we'll have to make contact with them. And so it's not something that can be done overnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The point I would like to make, Ms. Korner, is this: That the argument that the Defence knew that Mr. Filipovic was going to give evidence, including evidence on this Patriotic League is an argument which applies to you as well in the sense that you also knew that you were going to produce Mr. Filipovic as a witness of the Prosecution and inter alia he would be giving evidence on the Patriotic League. So basically if the statements of Mr. Halilovic contained information which was exculpatory pertaining to the Patriotic League or related -- related matters, I don't think it -- the fact --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the greatest respect, how on earth are we supposed to know that there's the slightest hint that Mr. Halilovic has got anything to do -- General Halilovic, whatever he is called, has got anything to do unless we're asked. I mean, we can search --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's being suggested to you now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know that. What I'm saying is it could have been -- should have been suggest sometime ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not necessarily. I mean, it depends when someone gets information. I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As you say, it seems -- it seems --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Regardless --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It seems that the information arrived today or --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I don't know that it did I'm guessing, because I saw Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But I think you're guessing right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if you show me the book, it means that it could have arrived earlier, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In any event, Your Honour, all I'm saying is this is not a simple matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know it's not a simple matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's most unlikely that if there is such material -- and I'm sorry, I don't understand what is it that they consider to be Rule 68 that Mr. Halilovic was a member of the Patriotic League. I think we're going to need a little more guidance on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I suppose -- let Mr. Ackerman speak -- sorry, Mr. Ackerman. Madam Fauveau was standing before you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Ms. Korner said we asked a year ago all of the exculpatory material which could be contained in the two cases related to Muslim generals. We have said that we are particularly interested in all the documents that prove the existence of Muslim units. And the Defence of General Talic couldn't have known that General Halilovic had given a statement. Now, if we had asked exculpatory elements in relation to this case that the statement of General Halilovic would enter into this category if it contained certain details relating to Muslim units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, by making this request, I'm not asking that the cross-examination of this witness be delayed while Ms. Korner is going through this process. The information, if it is what I believe it might be, can be useful on other parts of the case, even in the Defence part of the case. So I'm not requesting any kind of a delay. So time is not an issue here. I can tell you that the part that I read was translated this morning, and I read it at noon. And I raised it at, I think, the first opportunity I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I haven't waited to ambush Ms. Korner or any such thing. But it seems to me that there is a rule that says it's the obligation of the Prosecutor to provide to the Defence evidence in the possession of the Prosecutor that's exculpatory to the accused, statements from accused are evidence. And the business that they have to get permission of his lawyers to disclose them to us is ridiculous. Statements of Mr. Delalic and Mr. Mucic, were admitted in evidence in the trial against them without the permission of their lawyers. They were made public without the permission of their lawyers. There's nothing -- there's no ownership interest in the lawyers. These are statements -- voluntary statements given to the Prosecutor. They're evidence. And they belong to the Prosecutor. And she can give them to us if they are relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think -- of course the statements made by Mr. Delalic and the rest were made -- given in evidence. They were statements within the trial, the process that involved them. What we're talking about is a totally separate process involving separate accused. May I say, Your Honour, a completely different time scale as well. The charges relate to 1995, I think. But Your Honour, that's a totally different matter from disclosing material relevant to a trial which has not begun and which is at the moment undergoing the pre-trial process in a different trial and as a result making public those matters. But Your Honour, at the moment we're all arguing slightly in a vacuum. I will have inquiries made as to whether within the interviews conducted with Halilovic or, I suppose, properly any of the other defendants, accused in the Muslim case, there is any -- at the moment all I'm being asked to do, so it's quite clear as I understand it, is look to see what, if anything, they said about the Patriotic League. Well, then, I'm sorry, I hear Mr. Ackerman. I need guidance. It's no good just a general what is Rule 68. What do the Defence consider for these purposes on the interview of Rule 68? We've asked this question before -- is Rule 68?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The guidance is the same guidance that you've been operating under as you determined everything else regarding Rule 68. That's your job. That's the Prosecutor's job, Your Honour. I shouldn't be talking to Ms. Korner. That's the Prosecutor's job to determine what is Rule 68. Anything that contradicts obviously the Prosecutor's theory of this case, anything that contradicts the testimony of witnesses that are being put on by the Prosecutor -- I shouldn't have to stand here and give Ms. Korner a lecture about what Rule 68 is and what exculpatory evidence is. Everybody in the world that tries cases, criminal cases, knows what exculpatory evidence is and what she'd like me to do is reveal my defence so that she can then decide what there's material that's relevant to what my defence is but I'm not going to do that. But I'm going to hold her to that standard. And what I'm afraid will happen, Your Honour, and what Rule 68 is designed to avoid is there will come a time when the statements of General Halilovic will probably be evidence in his case or some other case become part of the trial record. And if we read those statements three or four years from now, when that happens, and find that they are filled with exculpatory material that should have been disclosed in this case, then we can seriously consider trying this case all over again, and that's what Rule 68 is designed to avoid. So that's what Ms. Korner's job is. Her job is to look at those statements. And if it contradicts her case, give it to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, I think the responsibility of this Chamber for the time being rests with making sure that the point raised by the two Defence teams, namely that they believe that there are statements by General Halilovic which contain exculpatory material which should be disclosed, is a point taken by the Prosecution which will follow up on that point and come back to either the two Defence teams directly or the Trial Chamber if there are difficulties that need to be smoothened or straightened out before a final decision is taken. But certainly it's not the case of the Trial Chamber receiving these document, going through them, and deciding for the Prosecution that it is exculpatory material or that it isn't exculpatory material at this very early stage, not even later, I suppose, because that's your discretion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, can I just make one other point. In the interests of not taking up time, it was perfectly open for Mr. Ackerman or Mr. Zecevic to raise this matter. I saw Mr. Ackerman earlier this morning or whatever outside court and ask us the question, rather than raising it with Your Honour, which tends to suggest there's going to be refusal. In my view, it's only necessary to bring these matters up before Your Honour. It's now of course in the public domain -- if, for example, we had refused or refused to make any inquiries, so Your Honour, I merely mention that at this stage. Mr. Ackerman in the 15 minutes before Your Honours came in when I was sitting here discussing other matters could have raised those matters with me. And I would urge that in the interest not of wasting time in court, not having this sort of discussion in open court, which is unnecessary, Defence counsel raise these matters with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, matters of this nature always need to be made of record because they may be important to future litigants regarding this case, and therefore that's why I do it that way. My private conversations with Ms. Korner is not part of the record and can't be read by some appellant lawyer and some other lawyer down the road. That's why they have to be part of the record, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Can we bring in the witness now. And by the way since definitely just for the record, the Rule 92 bis decision should be available by the -- by now. We handed it down today. That regards Kljuc municipality. The other one will follow as soon as I get this updated report on the risk assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The same procedure as yesterday. Could you please repeat your solemn declaration to tell us the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- our apologies for starting late. We started on time, but we had some procedural preliminaries to thrash before we could proceed with your testimony. Ms. Korner will take over from where she left yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I thought Your Honour wanted to ask about the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes. Now, yesterday you will recall, Mr. Filipovic, when you started giving evidence I asked you a couple of questions with regard to the video recording that you brought with you and which you handed to the Prosecution and which we haven't seen as yet. And I asked you specifically whether you knew who the commentator was, and you told us basically two things: Number one is that from the video recording itself, we -- you are in a position to identify the commentator because he's shown somewhere in the course of this video recording, and you also said that he is a gentleman with a bald head. And then you also said that at the end of the video recording there is his name. You're not -- you were not in a position to tell us his name just like that because you couldn't remember it, but you said that his name appears at the end of the video recording of this documentary. Do you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, because I cannot know his name. While he was making this programme, I was in the Manjaca concentration camp. And I have seen the video recording, and I can show you when he appears who he is. I can show him to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. Do you know whether he appears in the beginning, in the middle, or towards the end of the video recording, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think towards the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So perhaps during the break, Ms. Korner, we can take up what we discussed earlier. And instead of a 15-minute we can have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to say yesterday you asked me about the name of the man who held the Galleria cafe. And I remembered last night. His name was Nikola Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the Serb.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... now receives the rent, and the place is in the hands of a Muslim, of a Bosniak. No?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So basically would you agree, Ms. Korner, to detail someone from your office to stay with the witness during the break and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, no, what will have to happen is he'll have to be taken to an area where there's a video rather than being --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know where.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we can organise that and I can arrange for an investigator and an interpreter so that can point it out and show him the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And then we can just have that clip shown here, and we can take it up from there and see to the rest. All right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would Your Honour just give me one moment while I just deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Filipovic. I'd like you to have back again the document we were looking at last thing yesterday, which is document P850. And if you could find -- on the translation it's page 13, but it's a part of the document that is headed "Assessment of the general and military and political situation in the municipality." I think you'll find it, at least if I'm right, on page -- it's got some numbers you'll see on the handwritten, 00574398. Is that headed "Assessment of the general military and political situation in the municipality"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. All right. I just want to pick out some parts of this. If you come to the paragraph that begins "There are not many Croats in the municipality, but they are definitely well connected and would join the Muslim units." Did any Croats join units set up by the Muslim TO?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they did not. But there were Croats who were in the regular police force and who refused to show loyalty to the SAO Bosnian Krajina and refused to sign to become their police officers. And I believe that had there been more intensive conflicts, they would certainly have joined our men.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It goes on to say this: "The Muslims of the Kljuc municipality are organised. The leadership of the MBO and SDA is also the military leadership." Was that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Well, let me see. I think it is, because the people who headed the political parties were at the same time in the defence staff, defence headquarters, so that is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then this: "They receive orders directly from Sarajevo." Again, was that a correct assessment?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know from where we would get our orders if not from Sarajevo. Sarajevo is the capital of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is where the government is. We couldn't get orders from Belgrade or from Amsterdam or London but only from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So the simple answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then the next sentence -- or the next part of the sentence: "They definitely have connections in Sanski Most and Prijedor." Did you have any meetings with the Muslims in Prijedor and/or Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you mean me personally or ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, you personally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did go to a meeting in Prijedor and also to Sanski Most. But these were more meetings of an informative nature, for us to see and familiarise ourselves with the situation over there. As far as I can recollect, I only went to one meeting in Prijedor, and I talked to Mr. Mirza Mujacic, who in those days was a member or actually a deputy in the state parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And we went there to appeal to him that as a deputy in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina he should put on the agenda the situation in our region.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Apart from that meeting, did others from your organisation, the MBO, attend other meetings in Prijedor or Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all of us in the region are more or less friends. And some real meetings for consultations were not held, but people would call us from Sanski Most. This is 30 kilometres from Kljuc. "Come to see what things were like." We went over there, had a cup of coffee, and that's it. I think my late brother and Asim Egrlic went to Mirzet, Karabeg, and other people in Sanski Most for meetings of some sort, for discussions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. There's some suggestion here of, as it were, a sort of plan, a get-together. Was there any agreement between the Muslims in Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Kljuc that there should be some kind of attack planned on the Serbs in those areas?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. Our plans were exclusively defence plans.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then the report goes on: "They are most likely aware of their handicap in certain areas where the settlements are surrounded by or in the immediate vicinity of the Serbian population (the town of Kljuc, Velecevo, Dubocani, Crnjani, Zgon, Humici, Gornji Budelj, et cetera) they do not have clear natural protection of the rear, such as Sisa, Manjaca, and Grmec. It would be safe to assume that they could evacuate a part of their population by relying on Sanski Most. Their initial action would be a firm hold on Velagici and Krasulje, with bigger activities in Sanica and Krasulje-Kamicak. They will not refrain from advancing on Peci, Prhovo, Kopjenica, and Humici." Was that an accurate assessment of, for example, that you had no natural protection in the rear?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a correct assessment. And our greatest handicap was that we didn't have any protection in the rear, as opposed to the Serbs who had the Yugoslav People's Army behind them plus the Bosnian mountains and the big cities. We simply had the people, who were left to their own devices to flee, to see where they would go, and only Mount Osljak was the only mountain where the people could hide in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then finally on that paragraph, before we get to item 2: "It is realistic to say that the Muslim and Croatian forces cannot even have an initial advantage." Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that, because we had -- because we had no intention of having an advantage.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. But presupposing that the author of this report is correct and you had had an intention of causing an uprising of some kind, would you agree that, as the author says, you couldn't have even had an initial advantage?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with the author of this text if everything he wrote yesterday was right, that we had battalions, companies, weapons, the kind of weapons they had. Then I would agree with his assessment, because in that part of the area, who starts first has the advantage. Using the language of sports, who scores the first goal, he is in the lead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, this author doesn't think even if you started first, you could have even an initial advantage, but goes on to say this: "It is not unlikely that they might succeed in causing initial confusion with their actions." In any event, if we leave that part and we go to the second part of this assessment: "In realistically assessing the situation, we have to count on the sense, experience, and the organisation of our Serbian people. The Serbian people believe in the SDS and we believe that the beginning of combat would bring about complete unity of all Serbs. "The main task of all the SDS staffs would be the regularly and intensely monitor the situation in this and the following period in time and to take measures to neutralise surprises and maintain organised work and activities in the entire region. "Under no circumstances are we to lose our grip on power, which in short means the following: We hold the leadership of the forces and control the activities of the public administration organs. We are to maintain a base and a firm foundation in the police organs, hold the management of companies, control traffic," et cetera, et cetera. From your knowledge of Kljuc and the area, was that an accurate assessment of the SDS, the Serb's position?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then there's the question raised of an attack on the SAO Krajina and what should happen. Finally, item 3 "Tasks." "The Kljuc local board and staff." The primary and immediate tasks are as follows: "Secure a timely mobilisation of all our forces, keep and maintain our rule while maintaining the necessary level of management and command; secure and maintain the mobilisation of the entire police force, of Serbian nationality, naturally; hold and secure the municipality assembly buildings, the PTT building, the police buildings, the medical centre," et cetera, "the forest products company, the Sana clothing factory, communal services," and so on and so forth. First of all, it states in the translation we've got "Sana clothing factory." Was there a Sana factory in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not that company. That company is in Bosanski Novi, the textile factory. And in Kljuc there is a construction company called Sana. And there was one plant in Ribnik, a textile plant, a small plant in Ribnicanka, but it wasn't called Sana.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I ask, in the original, does it actually state "clothing factory"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it says "GP Sana", which means construction company Sana. That is the abbreviation for a construction company, GP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we ought to just mark that that's an erroneous translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, aside from that point, Mr. Filipovic, this is what they said had to happen. Was this in fact what happened in Kljuc? Was there mobilisation and mobilisation of the entire police force?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All companies, the executives -- the executive positions were held by Serbs. So all the things that you have listed so far are correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then if we go over the page, there are a number of points that are raised. But we see the words "Cover the entire town with police forces using Serbian buildings, apartments, and houses, with the initial focus on the already determined tasks of peacetime police." Before your arrest, Mr. Filipovic, on the 29th of May, was the town covered with police forces?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A correction. I was arrested on the 28th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the 28th.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 28th of May. And before that, apart from the regular police force, Kljuc was flooded with reservists, reserve policemen. And to a considerable extent, as I said yesterday in my testimony, we call them Knindzas, these were men with red berets. We gave them this nickname, ninja. We called them Knindzas because of Knin. They were attached to them. They were not local inhabitants of Kljuc. And I think there was a platoon of them, about 30 men strong. So the regular police force, the reserve police force, plus these 30 Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did you yourself hear these men speak, these Red Berets, any of them?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you able to tell where they came from?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell because I didn't have any documents. But judging by their accent, they spoke the Ekavica. But I can't assert that either, because in those days when the SDS took over power, all Serbs more or less switched to the Ekavica, because whoever did not speak Ekavica and who didn't write in Cyrillic was considered to be a poor Serb. In the last 50 years, 99 per cent of Serbs wrote the Latin script. And suddenly in the 1990's, everyone started writing in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then under that we see "Maintain roads in Kljuc and the exit from Kljuc, especially paying attention to exits towards Sisa." Anyhow, I asked you yesterday about barricades, and you said they weren't erected until the end of May. Were there checkpoints though, before the end of May set up?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were checkpoints. As far as I can remember, there was at the entrance to Kljuc on the bridge, then at the exit to Kljuc, at the turning for Sanski Most, at the turning for Sanica, at the entrance to Sanica, and down there close to the stadium. That is as much as I can remember, because movement was restricted so that we avoided moving around. But those I have just listed were checkpoints for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when did they start to be set up roughly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Roughly at what period of time were these checkpoints established?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the course of the month of May. At the time -- I think even before the takeover of the police administration on the 7th of May, but certainly from 7th of May onwards. But I think it happened even before, but I'm certain about it happening from 7th of May onwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was there ever an occasion when you ignored the checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, once.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what happened on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was going with my late brother for Dzenaza to Sanica. And we were left before we left Kljuc, we were checked four times and as we were going back, we were supposed to go through the same procedure, get a detailed check. If there was an airport, they would search the car. We would be searched. Even if they were just neighbours and friends, they knew who we were, there would be a detailed check. And as we were going back from Sanica, I said to my brother, "Shall we have a joke," and he said, "Why not?" So as they put out the sign to stop, I slowed down because I was driving. And the policeman as he approached, when he came a few metres from me, a couple metres from me, I then accelerated and then I went all the way -- drove all the way to the Kljuc checkpoint. As we arrived in Kljuc, they must have called Vinko, the chief, and Vinko was very angry and said, "Why didn't you shoot?"

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how did you hear that Vinko had said to the people at the checkpoints, "Why didn't you shoot?"

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he said that because Atif Dedic was at a checkpoint as a member, which means that situation with us happened before the 7th of May. Atif Dedic was there, as a policeman, a regular policeman. And as a reservist from the army was a man by the surname of Sirar. I don't know his first name. And I found out about Atif Dedic. That he said that to Vinko. And I said to Vinko, "You would have killed your colleague," and Vinko tried to justify and said that this wasn't true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. You can put that document away now. Now, I want to move, then, back to -- or I want to keep on going through the events of April and May. Could you please be shown now document P892.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] We saw this yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think so, Your Honour. But I may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This document is undated, but it's addressed -- and I think --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I will be corrected if I'm wrong, but I don't have a note that this is objected to, although it's not signed or dated. In any event, while Madam Fauveau is checking that -- but I went through her list, and I don't recall marking this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's addressed to the Kljuc Municipal Board -- oh, I'm sorry, the Serbian Democratic Party, municipal of Kljuc, notification of a meeting of the SDS Sokolovo local board. Now, again, could you have the map that you looked at yesterday, which is -- that's a name that comes up a number of times in these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's 1097. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we could just put that on the ELMO and if you could point out roughly where that is. We may have to use an alternate Serbian map, I think, at some stage.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Donji Sokolovo. And this is the village of Crljeni. Donji Sokolovo is located by the regional road between Kljuc and Sanski Most, while a few kilometres up the hill is the local road leading to the village of Crljeni. I think there's about 5 or 6 kilometres from Sokolovo to Crljeni.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. And this is a report that "There are a large number of weapons in the village of Crljeni, mostly automatic, which have been distributed to the population already included in guard watches. It was also discovered that those engaged on guard watch are paid. They even have a commander and a guard shift leader. Also stressed that the village has about 70 submachine-guns and one light machine-gun. We also found out from the villagers that the following persons are involved." And it names the people. I'll come back to that in a moment. And then says: "We wish to draw your attention to the fact that the Serbian people in this area are really under threat. The people ask you to understand this serious situation and immediately undertake everything within your power to address this issue." First, the people that are named, did you know them, Mr. Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I know Kemal Dedic, I know Muhedin Hrustic, I know Miralem Medic, I know Jusuf Omerovic, and I know Latif Omerovic not so well. But the ones I've mentioned, I know them well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is said that they had about 70 submachine-guns and one light machine-gun. Now, do you know whether or not that was true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what makes you say that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because if we had had in only one village so many weapons. Here you can put a map up on here and we can see how many villages. Now, if we had -- really would have had all the weapons that the SDS claimed that we had. And out of this, most of the weapons were hunting rifles, old-fashioned pistols, handguns with permits. And I'm not saying that somebody didn't have an automatic or a semi-automatic rifle, which they bought from JNA members.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was anybody in your organisation, the MBO, responsible within the Crisis Staff of the Patriotic League -- responsible for keeping a list of what weapons were available to the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you, we did have -- we knew about it. We knew what weapons we had. When I mentioned earlier when I went to see Mr. Mujacic, we particularly went to see him on this matter to ask from Sarajevo Territorial Defence weapons, but the Serbs preempted us and they took the Territorial Defence weapons to Kula. And the Territorial Defence weapons belonged to Muslims, Serbs, and Croats. These are not the weapons owned by the JNA but these are the weapons owned by the town of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But you said you went to ask for help but you were preempted. Was anybody actually saying, "This is what we know we have available for the Muslim population"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who do you mean said that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Was there anybody that you're aware of who was responsible for keeping a record, a written record, of what weapons were available to members of the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't keep a list and records, but we knew roughly what we had because we had contact with people, so we knew when a person had a rifle, anyone who bought a rifle would say, "I have a rifle." Everybody knew. In my statement I said that there were five to seven hundred guns that we had, and this would include automatic rifles, old-fashioned pistols, handguns, and hunting rifles. This is according to the records that we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Korner. Mr. Filipovic, could I kindly ask you to read the penultimate paragraph, the one which starts [B/C/S spoken]. Could you read it aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "We have listed here just some individuals. Out of the total number of persons involved, that's about 70 people."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because this is missing in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps if you knew these -- the persons you mentioned out of the list that shows -- is shown in this document, would you agree that the -- in the organisation itself there were about 70 members? Would you agree that there were 70?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To tell you the truth, the whole village was involved in the organisation, men, women, and children, although men were more exposed. And now to tell you where Crljeni is, to tell you here in The Hague, I have to say that Crljeni is just a drop in the ocean surrounded by the Serb territory. It's like a very, very small pond in the Netherlands. This is what Crljeni is. And according to my estimate, without any census data from 1991 how many inhabitants there were, I believe that they were unable to do anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry, Your Honour, I just noticed that the next documents I think are out of place. I'm going to skip them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Can we come, please -- could you be shown Exhibit P167. It comes after the second divider 10, and it follows on from 897. This is a decision of the autonomous -- the Secretariat for National Defence. And it is stamped on the other side and signed secretary of the regional secretariat for National Defence, Colonel Miodrag Sajic. Did you know who Colonel Sajic was, Mr. Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is dated the 4th of May, the decision. It calls for public mobilisation, introduces a curfew in paragraph 4, and then in paragraph 5, "All paramilitary formations and individuals in possession of illegal weapons and ammunition are asked to surrender these weapons -- or those weapons and ammunition immediately, or not later than 1500 hours on the 11th of May, 1992." And I don't think you need trouble with the rest. Now, do you recall, first of all, a -- the SAO Krajina calling for general public mobilisation at the beginning of May?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that the mobilisation was public, but the mobilisation started when the war in Croatia started, so there was always mobilisation, always new recruits were mobilised to leave. So I don't know whether we as Muslims had publicly said that we were refusing to join such an army, so I wasn't really interested in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, page 35, line 4 says that Ms. Korner asked the question "do you recall the SAO Krajina calling for general public mobilisation." This document doesn't say anything about SAO Krajina. In fact, there was no organisation as SAO Krajina. And so it's a misstatement of the evidence or a mistake in the transcript. I'm not sure which.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ackerman -- this is Mr. Ackerman's ploy to say it's a mistake in the transcript. I said and Mr. Ackerman heard me say and indeed I heard his legal assistant tell him something about this. Your Honour, I apologise. I will read out what is in the translation if these technical points are to be taken. What the document is headed is "The Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina republic secretariat for National Defence. The number is 01-1/92. The date is the 4th of May, 1992. And the decision which apparently is pursuant to a decision of the 16th of April, 1992 of the Ministry of National Defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is: 1. A call for general, public mobilisation on the entire territory of what is said to be the AP Krajina." However, you've already dealt -- however I called it, Mr. Filipovic, you've dealt with that. But can I ask you about the second paragraph -- I'm sorry, the fifth paragraph in this decision. The call for disarmament of paramilitary formations and individuals in possession of illegal weapons. They should be surrendered by -- immediately or by the 11th of May, 1992. Do you recall any announcement being made in Kljuc that there should be a surrender of what were termed "illegal weapons and ammunition"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. But I know we didn't pay attention to this because we believed that everything that was being done here was illegal at that time. So very quickly, after that you can see here the date is 4th of May, 1992, three days later. There was the takeover of the police. And from then on everything else that I spoke about came into force.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You can leave that document now. Thank you very much. Now, I want you to look, please, at the next document in the bundle, P898.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, again this comes from the Croatian state archives, not the 1st Krajina Corps, although it is -- it does bear a stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We contest this document for the same reasons. We don't know what the chain of custody was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. And I understand what you said earlier, applicable to the other document would apply to this document as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown will deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look at the date. The document is dated the same day as the document we've just looked at, the 4th of May, 1992. And it's signed or -- I'm sorry, it bears the name at the end of Colonel Galic. "Situations in unit. A reconnaissance platoon of the 30th Partisan Division was formed of 52 volunteers from the broader Kljuc municipality area." And then over the page, please, in the translation but paragraph 6. "State of morale." The paragraph -- the second part of the paragraph reads as follows: "Could you please intervene through the Krajina government to exert its influence on representatives of the authorities in Kljuc. Serbian extremism is increasingly present there, induced by the official organs of authority, since the president of the municipality is asking to have his own army which he would use as he sees fit. This must be resolved urgently." This was the -- the report was apparently being sent to the command of the 5th Corps. Now, were you aware of Mr. Banjac asking to have his own army?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he requested that, but what he did certainly went in that direction. He was working on that, to make some kind of a unit, that is, a Kljuc unit, whereby he would be the commander of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And presumably the sentence "Serbian extremism is increasingly present there," would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree completely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. If we then look on the same topic at the next document, P899, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this does come from the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is dated the following day, the 5th of May. It's addressed to the 30th Partisan Brigade command. And it seems to be a reply to the previous report. It talks about the bridge in Donji Vakuf which was mentioned and the transmitter in the wider area of Kljuc have recently been destroyed. Now, by the 5th of May, had a transmitter been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The repeater wasn't destroyed. It was broken. The equipment -- I'm not an expert in this matter, but the equipment was broken so that it made it impossible to follow the second channel. But there was still -- the pillar was still there on the Ramicki Kamen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, Your Honour. I think I'll have to go back to the previous document because I did miss out a part that this makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you have back, please, 898. I'm sorry. If we look at 3, "Situation in the territory." "Following the destruction of the bridge in Donji Vakuf, most of the town's inhabitants of Muslim nationality and many of Serbian nationality left, and now there is practically nobody in charge in the town." Then if you go over the page in the translation: "The problems in connection with the Kljuc municipality are worsening due to the murder of another Muslim in the village of Sehovci on the 3rd of May, 1992, when Senad Dervisevic -- I think I'll give that one up -- son of Ibrahim was murdered by military conscript, Pero Grujicic, son of Milutin, from the village of Purici-Sitnica. The murder was committed while under the influence of alcohol." Very briefly, did you know about that murder, Mr. Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know about it. The murder didn't happen in Sehici, but the murder took place, as I explained yesterday, near the bus station on the main street, Masala Tita Street, and very near the Galleria coffee bar. Dervisevic Senad was killed. And yesterday I said that everything ended by the statement that a drunken soldier had come from the front exhausted, and after that we felt like feeling what will happen to us if Serb soldiers come back from the front, come back tired. So people started to stay at home, to go home and hide, as the Serb soldiers were coming back from the front.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The last sentence wasn't heard by the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The interpreter didn't hear the last sentence. The -- what we have here -- "so people started to stay at home, to go home and hide, as the Serb soldiers were coming back from the front." Then you went on to say something else, another sentence. Could you remember what you'd said, so the interpreters can translate it to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I went to his funeral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, sir. Whenever it's -- I think you can go to the transmitter thing now, which is the next sentence, then refer to 899, and we'll have a break after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "The TV repeater on the Osljak relay station in the village of Ramici was sabotaged, and as a result there is no TV signal reception in the Kljuc area. The sabotage was carried out by Muslim extremists in response to the capture of the transmitter on Mount Vlasic."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just going ask one question on that, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The description of Muslim extremists. Who did sabotage this relay station?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you know.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know one person, Emin Pejic. He was such an extremist. He's even now in prison at the Zenica penitentiary. He is a young man with a criminal file. And he as a criminal didn't like what he was seeing on TV, so on his own initiative he went without anyone's order and he went and destroyed this equipment so you could still follow the first channel of Sarajevo television but you couldn't follow the second channel of -- so that would have been Belgrade TV.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I think you may have answered the question, but was this on any orders of any Muslim leaders that the relay was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we'll make arrangements over the break for Mr. Filipovic to watch the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will have now a 20-minute break, extendable as you make an assessment of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, would you -- I think if you say 25 minutes. He'd have to go upstairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 25 minutes break. If you need more so that you make sure he can identify which parts of the video recording we need to see, then obviously -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I apologise they had to ask for more time. We had a slight --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic has watched the video together with an interpreter and investigator, has identified the part where you can see the reporter. He can't -- he doesn't know what his name is, but he says he can find out probably if it's so required. There are no credits as such on the tape, but it mentions that it's from TV Banja Luka. So that's the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Are from any comments from Mr. Ackerman or Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't -- I've not seen what the witness thinks is a picture of the commentator, and so I don't know what it is. If it's -- I mean, how does he know that the picture is a picture of the person who actually did the commentating on the tape? Because he was in Manjaca when the whole thing was done and I don't know how he would know. He's apparently identified a picture of some bald guy, but how can he say that's the person whose voice is the commentary, as he said, he wasn't there. He was in Manjaca. He has no idea. And so -- I don't know. Maybe if we saw that segment of the tape we would all draw that conclusion, but I'm not certain we would. I haven't seen it, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why don't we ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. In fact, that's what I was going so do. Do you have any remarks to make having heard what Mr. Ackerman had to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the observation by Mr. Ackerman is out of place and it is suited to a six-month-old child. It's sufficient to see the video to know who is the commentator, and therefore I stand by what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if Mr. Ackerman thinks I'm a fool, then let it be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't need to insult Mr. Ackerman, and I will stop you if you try to do that. The lawyers are here to do their duty. They have their clients to defend, and I will allow them to defend their clients according to law. But I will stop you if you do anything which is not according to law. And calling a lawyer that his remark is that of a six-year-old child is very offensive, and I wouldn't expect it from someone like you. I hope you got the message from me, because if you do that, we will suddenly be on a head-on collision course, you and I.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I, too, am a person, and therefore Mr. Ackerman cannot accuse me of certain things. If the law applies to me, it applies to you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We simply asked you to explain. We asked you to explain, and that's it. So can we see the relevant part from the video recording, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it will have to go to the AV unit. It's on -- if they start the counter at nought and run to 2419 according to our counter -- and I know that not all counters are the same -- that should show why Mr. Filipovic says that's the reporter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When the usher comes back, if the screen is done for Mr. Filipovic, and if he just says "forward" or "back."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, if -- when -- I think you have to -- does he remain on "video monitor", or does he go on "computer monitor" now, at this --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He goes on to "video" now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You go on "video monitor." The usher will perhaps help you with that. Now, Mr. Filipovic, what's going to happen is the technician is going to start relaying the video from where we told him to start from. Now, that may be either precise, correct, or else a little bit before or a little bit after. If we need to go back, please tell us so that we go backwards a little bit. We do -- a rewind procedure. I'm still waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I've already been to the doctor once today to -- to have my neck checked. I don't want to go again to have my eyes checked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, what's happened is -- I'm sorry, a complete misunderstanding. The video was set up from where it should start, they've taken it back to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Ms. Korner. Microphone. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The video was -- [French interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm hearing someone talking in French.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm getting French now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: My apology. My apology. The French interpreter was on the English channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. It's -- okay. Please make my life a little bit more easy. Ms. Korner tried to explain that she had -- that the tape was set -- Okay. Madam Chuqing is clarifying that. I think we are still in time to be able to go back, to revert.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If Your Honour the technicians go -- take it -- I've had -- I don't know why. Each time we set up a video from the place that it should start, something goes wrong. It's now going to be much more difficult, but if you run it roughly forward for 20 minutes or so where the beginning of the sequence is that deals with the members of the Crisis Staff talking. It's about 20 minutes. Put that at nought and then run 24 on from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Has that reached the technician, that explanation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it after this, Mr. Filipovic? Do you remember whether this -- what we are seeing now -- came before or after?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it should be wound forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An armoured checkpoint -- a checkpoint should appear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we try fast-forwarding?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. It's supposed to -- I think it's being fast-forwarded, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Kondic is very loquacious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you fast-forward it without us having to see this? Because I understand from the little that I know that when you fast-forward not having the picture on, it's much faster. This is all your fault, Mr. Ackerman. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will just take whatever punishment I deserve for it, Your Honour. I'm prepared.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Perhaps the instruction from Madam Korner is not that helpful. If we stop the picture, then the technician couldn't spot where we should stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I didn't give that instruction. I'm told, however, that if they take it -- if we stop this whole thing again, go back to the beginning so that it's at nought, and then run it for 44 minutes, that roughly we hope they get -- they've got a copy upstairs. So I think the answer is go back, run it right back as they did to the beginning, and then try at around 44 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there. Stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. Go back a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is this the -- this is where you want us to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the reporter. You asked me to show you the person -- the interviewer in this programme, and this was the commentator, the moderator of this whole broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
